Explanation.—For the purpose of this section, claims enforceable under an attachment include claims for the rateable distribution of assets.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once property is attached, the judgment-debtor cannot secretly sell, transfer, or hand it over to someone else, nor can a third party pay the debtor money owed to them in a way that defeats the attachment — any such attempt is void against attachment claims. The one carve-out is a transfer made under a contract that was both entered into and registered before the attachment happened.
essential_elements: Applies to private transfers or delivery of attached property (or any interest in it), and to payments of debts/dividends/monies to the judgment-debtor made contrary to the attachment.
Such transfers/payments are void as against all claims enforceable under the attachment, including claims for rateable distribution of assets.
Exception: a transfer made under a contract that was both entered into and registered before the attachment is unaffected.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The registered-contract exception is narrow — it requires both execution and registration of the contract to predate the attachment, not merely an informal prior agreement.
breakdown.how_to_read: The anti-evasion backbone of the attachment regime — pair with Section 63's Explanation on rateable distribution and with Order XXI's attachment procedure when advising a decree-holder worried about the debtor dissipating assets.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: एक बार संपत्ति कुर्क हो जाने पर, निर्णय-ऋणी गुप्त रूप से उसे किसी और को बेच, हस्तांतरित या सौंप नहीं सकता, न ही कोई तीसरा पक्ष ऋणी को देय धन इस प्रकार चुका सकता है जो कुर्की को विफल करे — ऐसा कोई भी प्रयास कुर्की दावों के विरुद्ध शून्य होगा। एकमात्र अपवाद ऐसे संविदा के तहत किया गया हस्तांतरण है जो कुर्की से पहले ही निष्पादित और पंजीकृत दोनों हो चुका था।
essential_elements_hi: कुर्क संपत्ति (या उसमें किसी हित) के निजी हस्तांतरण या सुपुर्दगी पर, और कुर्की के विपरीत निर्णय-ऋणी को किए गए ऋण/लाभांश/धन के भुगतान पर लागू।
ऐसे हस्तांतरण/भुगतान कुर्की के तहत प्रवर्तनीय सभी दावों के विरुद्ध शून्य हैं, जिसमें आस्तियों के आनुपातिक वितरण के दावे शामिल हैं।
अपवाद: ऐसे संविदा के तहत किया गया हस्तांतरण जो कुर्की से पहले ही निष्पादित और पंजीकृत दोनों हो चुका था, अप्रभावित रहता है।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: पंजीकृत-संविदा अपवाद संकीर्ण है — इसके लिए संविदा का निष्पादन और पंजीकरण दोनों कुर्की से पहले होना आवश्यक है, मात्र एक अनौपचारिक पूर्व करार पर्याप्त नहीं।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: कुर्की व्यवस्था की धोखाधड़ी-विरोधी रीढ़ — आनुपातिक वितरण पर धारा 63 के स्पष्टीकरण और आदेश XXI की कुर्की प्रक्रिया के साथ जोड़कर देखें जब किसी डिक्रीदार को सलाह दें जो ऋणी द्वारा आस्तियाँ नष्ट किए जाने को लेकर चिंतित हो।

sections.title: Purchaser's title.
sections.raw_text: Where immovable property is sold in execution of a decree and such sale has become absolute, the property shall be deemed to have vested in the purchaser from the time when the property is sold and not from the time when the sale becomes absolute.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once an execution sale of immovable property is confirmed (becomes absolute), the law treats the purchaser as having owned the property from the moment of the actual sale — not merely from the later date of confirmation — giving the purchaser's title retroactive effect back to the sale date.
essential_elements: Applies to sales of immovable property in execution of a decree.
Operative only once the sale has become absolute (i.e., confirmed under the applicable execution rules).
Title is deemed to vest in the purchaser retroactively from the date of sale, not from the later date of confirmation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Important for tracing title disputes and for computing limitation/possession periods in cases involving auction-purchased immovable property — the relevant date is the sale date, not the confirmation date.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: एक बार अचल संपत्ति की निष्पादन-बिक्री पुष्ट (अंतिम) हो जाने पर, कानून खरीदार को वास्तविक बिक्री के क्षण से ही संपत्ति का स्वामी मानता है — न कि केवल बाद की पुष्टिकरण तिथि से — जिससे खरीदार के स्वामित्व को बिक्री तिथि तक पूर्वव्यापी प्रभाव मिलता है।
essential_elements_hi: डिक्री के निष्पादन में अचल संपत्ति की बिक्री पर लागू।
केवल तभी प्रभावी जब बिक्री अंतिम हो गई हो (अर्थात् लागू निष्पादन नियमों के तहत पुष्ट हो गई हो)।
स्वामित्व खरीदार में पूर्वव्यापी रूप से बिक्री की तिथि से निहित माना जाता है, न कि बाद की पुष्टिकरण तिथि से।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: नीलामी-क्रीत अचल संपत्ति से जुड़े मामलों में स्वामित्व विवादों का पता लगाने और परिसीमा/कब्ज़ा अवधि की गणना के लिए महत्वपूर्ण — प्रासंगिक तिथि बिक्री तिथि है, पुष्टिकरण तिथि नहीं।

sections.title: [Suit purchase being on behalf of plaintiff.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1988 (45 of 1988), section 7, with effect from 19 May 1988. This section formerly dealt with the position where property was purchased at an execution sale in the name of one person but on behalf of another (a decree-holder), including restrictions on suits challenging the real ownership of such purchases.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 66 is no longer in force. It used to regulate suits challenging benami-style execution-sale purchases made nominally in one person's name but actually on behalf of the decree-holder or another.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 19 May 1988.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: A stub entry preserving section-number contiguity — do not cite this as live law.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 66 अब प्रभावी नहीं है। यह उन वादों को नियंत्रित करती थी जो नाम मात्र किसी एक व्यक्ति के नाम पर, किंतु वास्तव में डिक्रीदार या किसी अन्य की ओर से की गई बेनामी-शैली की निष्पादन-बिक्री खरीद को चुनौती देते थे।
essential_elements_hi: 19 मई 1988 से औपचारिक रूप से निरसित।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: यहाँ केवल क्रमांक-निरंतरता बनाए रखने हेतु रखा गया है; इसका अब कोई विधिक प्रभाव नहीं है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: धारा-क्रमांक निरंतरता बनाए रखने वाली एक रिक्त प्रविष्टि — इसे प्रचलित कानून के रूप में उद्धृत न करें।

sections.title: Power for State Government to make rules as to sales of land in execution of decrees for payment of money.
sections.raw_text:
(1) The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for any local area imposing conditions in respect of the sale of any class of interests in land in execution of decrees for the payment of money, where such interests are so uncertain or undetermined as, in the opinion of the State Government, to make it impossible to fix their value.
(2) When on the date on which this Code came into operation in any local area, any special rules as to sale of land in execution of decrees were in force therein, the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare such rules to be in force, or may by a like notification, modify the same. Every notification issued in the exercise of the powers conferred by this sub-section shall set out the rules so continued or modified.
(3) Every rule made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before the State Legislature.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the value of a land interest is too uncertain or undetermined to fix normally (making an ordinary sale-in-execution impractical), the State Government can make special rules by Gazette notification governing how such interests are sold to satisfy money decrees, and can continue or modify any pre-existing local special rules on the same subject.
essential_elements: Power applies specifically to interests in land whose uncertainty/indeterminacy makes valuation impossible, in the State Government's opinion.
Rules are made by notification in the Official Gazette and apply to a specified local area.
Pre-existing special local sale rules in force when the Code commenced may be continued or modified by similar notification.
Every rule made under this section must be laid before the State Legislature.
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow rule-making power for an edge case (unvaluable land interests) — mostly relevant in areas with unusual tenurial arrangements; check for a State-specific notification before assuming ordinary Order XXI sale procedure applies.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: जहाँ भूमि हित का मूल्य इतना अनिश्चित या अनिर्धारित हो कि सामान्य रूप से तय न किया जा सके (जिससे सामान्य निष्पादन-बिक्री अव्यावहारिक हो जाए), राज्य सरकार राजपत्र अधिसूचना द्वारा ऐसे हितों को धन-डिक्री संतुष्ट करने हेतु बेचने के विशेष नियम बना सकती है, और इसी विषय पर किसी पूर्व-विद्यमान स्थानीय विशेष नियम को जारी रख सकती है या संशोधित कर सकती है।
essential_elements_hi: शक्ति विशेष रूप से ऐसे भूमि हितों पर लागू होती है जिनकी अनिश्चितता/अनिर्धारणीयता के कारण, राज्य सरकार की राय में, मूल्यांकन असंभव हो।
नियम राजपत्र में अधिसूचना द्वारा बनाए जाते हैं और किसी निर्दिष्ट स्थानीय क्षेत्र पर लागू होते हैं।
संहिता के प्रारंभ होने के समय लागू पूर्व-विद्यमान विशेष स्थानीय बिक्री नियमों को समान अधिसूचना द्वारा जारी रखा या संशोधित किया जा सकता है।
इस धारा के तहत बनाया गया हर नियम राज्य विधानमंडल के समक्ष रखा जाना चाहिए।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: एक अपवाद मामले (अमूल्यांकनीय भूमि हित) के लिए संकीर्ण नियम-निर्माण शक्ति — अधिकतर असामान्य धारणाधिकार व्यवस्थाओं वाले क्षेत्रों में प्रासंगिक; सामान्य आदेश XXI बिक्री प्रक्रिया मान लेने से पहले राज्य-विशिष्ट अधिसूचना की जाँच करें।

sections.title: [Power to prescribe rules for transferring to collector execution of certain decrees.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1956 (66 of 1956), section 7, with effect from 1 January 1957. This section, together with Sections 69 to 72, formerly formed a scheme permitting execution of certain decrees against immovable property to be transferred to the Collector for execution under special rules, rather than through the ordinary civil court process.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 68 is no longer in force. It used to let the State Government make rules transferring execution of certain decrees against immovable property to the Collector instead of the civil court.
essential_elements: Formally repealed with effect from 1 January 1957.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Retained here only as a numbering placeholder; it has no current legal effect.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of a now wholly repealed Collector-execution scheme (Sections 68-72) — see the repeal notes on Sections 69-72 for the rest of the scheme.
breakdown.plain_summary_hi: धारा 68 अब प्रभावी नहीं है। यह राज्य सरकार को अचल संपत्ति के विरुद्ध कुछ डिक्रियों के निष्पादन को सिविल न्यायालय के बजाय कलेक्टर को हस्तांतरित करने के नियम बनाने देती थी।
essential_elements_hi: 1 जनवरी 1957 से औपचारिक रूप से निरसित।
exceptions_and_qualifications_hi: यहाँ केवल क्रमांक-निरंतरता बनाए रखने हेतु रखा गया है; इसका अब कोई विधिक प्रभाव नहीं है।
breakdown.how_to_read_hi: अब पूर्णतः निरसित कलेक्टर-निष्पादन योजना (धारा 68-72) का हिस्सा — शेष योजना के लिए धारा 69-72 पर निरसन टिप्पणियाँ देखें।

sections.title: [Provisions of Third Schedule to apply.] Repealed.

sections.title: Proceeds of execution-sale to be rateably distributed among decree-holders.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where assets are held by a Court and more persons than one have, before the receipt of such assets, made application to the Court for the execution of decrees for the payment of money passed against the same judgment-debtor and have not obtained satisfaction thereof, the assets, after deducting the costs of realization, shall be rateably distributed among all such persons:
Provided as follows:—
(a) where any property is sold subject to a mortgage or charge, the mortgagee or incumbrancer shall not be entitled to share in any surplus arising from such sale;
(b) where any property liable to be sold in execution of a decree is subject to a mortgage or charge, the Court may, with the consent of the mortgagee or incumbrancer, order that the property be sold free from the mortgage or charge, giving to the mortgagee or incumbrancer the same interest in the proceeds of the sale as he had in the property sold;
(c) where any immovable property is sold in execution of a decree ordering its sale for the discharge of an incumbrance thereon, the proceeds of sale shall be applied — First, in defraying the expenses of the sale; Secondly, in discharging the amount due under the decree; Thirdly, in discharging the interest and principal monies due on subsequent incumbrances (if any); and Fourthly, rateably among the holders of decrees for the payment of money against the judgment-debtor, who have, prior to the sale of the property, applied to the Court which passed the decree ordering such sale for execution of such decrees, and have not obtained satisfaction thereof.
(2) Where all or any of the assets liable to be rateably distributed under this section are paid to a person not entitled to receive the same, any person so entitled may sue such person to compel him to refund the assets.
(3) Nothing in this section affects any right of the Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a court is holding money recovered from a judgment-debtor and several different decree-holders (with separate money decrees against that same debtor) have all applied for execution before the money came in, the court doesn't pay whoever applied first in full — it divides the assets proportionately (rateably) among all of them, after deducting realization costs. Special rules apply where the property was mortgaged or charged.
essential_elements: Applies where a court holds assets and multiple decree-holders, each with unsatisfied money decrees against the same judgment-debtor, applied for execution before those assets were received.
After deducting realization costs, the assets are distributed rateably (proportionately) among all such applicants.
A mortgagee/incumbrancer whose secured property was sold does not share in any surplus from that sale (proviso (a)).
With the mortgagee's consent, property may be sold free of the mortgage, with the mortgagee's interest shifting to the sale proceeds instead (proviso (b)).

Where property is sold specifically to discharge an incumbrance, proceeds go first to sale expenses, then the decree amount, then subsequent incumbrances, and only then rateably among other money-decree holders who applied before the sale (proviso (c)).
A person who wrongly receives assets that should have been rateably distributed can be sued by the rightful claimant to compel a refund.
The section does not affect any right of the Government (which retains its own priority elsewhere in law).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rateable distribution requires the competing applications to have been made before the assets were actually received by the court — later applicants do not automatically share.
breakdown.how_to_read: The key equitable-sharing rule among competing money-decree holders — read with Section 63 (multi-court attachment priority) and Section 64 (void private alienation) as the trio governing multi-claimant execution scenarios.

sections.title: Resistance to execution.
sections.raw_text: Where the Court is satisfied that the holder of a decree for the possession of immovable property or that the purchaser of immovable property sold in execution of a decree has been resisted or obstructed in obtaining possession of the property by the judgment-debtor or some person on his behalf and that such resistance or obstruction was without any just cause, the Court may, at the instance of the decree-holder or purchaser, order the judgment-debtor or such other person to be detained in the civil prison for a term which may extend to thirty days and may further direct that the decree-holder or purchaser be put into possession of the property.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a judgment-debtor (or someone acting for them) blocks the decree-holder or auction-purchaser from actually taking possession of immovable property they're legally entitled to, and the court finds this obstruction had no genuine justification, the court can jail the obstructor for up to thirty days and order that the decree-holder or purchaser be physically given possession.
essential_elements: Applies to resistance or obstruction in obtaining possession of immovable property, whether by a decree-holder or an execution-sale purchaser.
The resistance/obstruction must be by the judgment-debtor or someone acting on their behalf.
The court must be satisfied the resistance was without any just cause.
Remedy: detention in civil prison for up to thirty days, plus a direction to put the decree-holder/purchaser into possession.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the resistance has a genuine/just cause (e.g. a bona fide third-party claim), this coercive remedy is not available — the matter typically proceeds through the investigation machinery in Order XXI instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: A frontline remedy for obstructive judgment-debtors in possession decrees — read alongside Order XXI Rules 97-103, which supply the fuller procedural machinery for resistance and dispossession disputes.

sections.title: Power of Court to issue commissions.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 75 opens Part III's 'Incidental Proceedings' by giving courts a general power to delegate specific fact-finding or administrative tasks to a court-appointed commissioner — from examining witnesses and investigating sites, to auditing accounts, dividing property, running expert investigations, selling perishable goods in custody, or handling routine ministerial acts.
essential_elements: The power to issue a commission is subject to prescribed conditions and limitations (fleshed out in Order XXVI).

Seven distinct purposes are listed: examining a person, local investigation, examining/adjusting accounts, partition, scientific/technical/expert investigation, sale of speedily-decaying property in court custody, and ministerial acts.
breakdown.how_to_read: The gateway provision for Order XXVI's detailed commission procedure — useful whenever a fact-finding task (site inspection, accounts, expert opinion) needs a court-appointed intermediary rather than direct oral evidence.

sections.title: Commission to another Court.
sections.raw_text:
(1) A commission for the examination of any person may be issued to any Court (not being a High Court) situate in a State other than the State in which the Court of issue is situate and having jurisdiction in the place in which the person to be examined resides.
(2) Every Court receiving a commission for the examination of any person under sub-section (1) shall examine him or cause him to be examined pursuant thereto, and the commission, when it has been duly executed, shall be returned together with the evidence taken under it to the Court from which it was issued, unless the order for issuing the commission has otherwise directed, in which case the commission shall be returned in terms of such order.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a witness lives in a different State from the trial court, that court can send a commission to a (non-High Court) court in the witness's State asking it to examine the witness; the receiving court conducts the examination and sends the evidence back to the issuing court.
essential_elements: The receiving court must not be a High Court and must be situated in a different State from the issuing court.
The receiving court must have jurisdiction over the place where the person to be examined resides.
The receiving court examines the person (or arranges for their examination) and returns the executed commission with the evidence to the issuing court, unless the issuing order directs otherwise.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read with Section 75(a) (the general power to issue a commission to examine a person) and Order XXVI for detailed procedure — Section 76 specifically addresses the inter-State transmission mechanics.

sections.title: Letter of request.
sections.raw_text: In lieu of issuing a commission the Court may issue a letter of request to examine a witness residing at any place not within India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Instead of a formal commission, a court can use a letter of request — essentially a diplomatic/judicial request — to get a witness residing outside India examined, typically through the foreign judicial system.
essential_elements: Available as an alternative to issuing a commission.
Applies specifically to witnesses residing outside India.
breakdown.how_to_read: The cross-border evidence-gathering tool of choice when a formal commission to a foreign court (Section 78 machinery) is impractical — commonly used in international commercial litigation.

sections.title: Commissions issued by foreign Courts.
sections.raw_text:
Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed the provisions as to the execution and return of commissions for the examination of witnesses shall apply to commissions issued by or at the instance of—
(a) Courts situate in any part of India to which the provisions of this Code do not extend; or
(b) Courts established or continued by the authority of the Central Government outside India; or
(c) Courts of any State or country outside India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 78 makes the Code's commission-execution machinery a two-way street: Indian courts must also execute and return commissions sent to them by courts in non-Code parts of India, by Indian-authority courts abroad, or by courts of other States/countries.
essential_elements: Applies to commissions issued by, or at the instance of, three categories of foreign/external courts: non-Code-territory Indian courts, Central-Government-established courts outside India, and courts of any foreign State or country.
Such commissions are executed and returned following the same provisions applicable to commissions issued by Indian courts, subject to prescribed conditions and limitations.
breakdown.how_to_read: The reciprocal counterpart to Sections 76-77 — completes the cross-border evidence framework by obligating Indian courts to assist foreign commissions, not just to send their own.

sections.title: Suits by or against Government.
sections.raw_text:
In a suit by or against the Government, the authority to be named as plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be, shall be—
(a) in the case of a suit by or against the Central Government, the Union of India, and
(b) in the case of a suit by or against a State Government, the State.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 79 fixes exactly who to name in the cause title when suing the Government: for the Central Government it is always 'the Union of India'; for a State Government it is simply 'the State' (i.e., the relevant State by name).
essential_elements: Suits involving the Central Government must name the Union of India as the plaintiff or defendant.
Suits involving a State Government must name the State (that specific State) as the plaintiff or defendant.
breakdown.how_to_read: A basic but frequently checked drafting rule — getting the cause-title party wrong (naming a ministry or department instead of the Union of India) is a common, avoidable defect that invites objections.

sections.title: Notice.

breakdown.plain_summary: Before suing the Government or a public officer for something done in their official capacity, Section 80 requires giving two months' advance written notice to the correct authority, spelling out the cause of action, plaintiff's details, and relief claimed — a cooling-off period meant to let the Government consider settling before litigation. Urgent cases can skip the wait with the court's leave, and minor notice defects don't automatically sink the suit if the core information got through.
essential_elements: The two-month notice requirement applies to suits against the Government or against a public officer for acts purporting to be done in official capacity.

Notice must be delivered/left at the office of the specified authority: a Secretary for the Central Government (or the Railway General Manager for railway matters), the J&K Chief Secretary or authorized officer, or a Secretary/Collector for other State Governments.
The notice must state the cause of action, the plaintiff's name/description/residence, and the relief claimed; the plaint must recite that notice was given.

Sub-section (2) allows bypassing notice, with the court's leave, for suits seeking urgent or immediate relief — but relief (interim or final) can only be granted after giving the Government/officer a reasonable opportunity to show cause.
If the court later finds no real urgency existed, it must return the plaint for re-presentation after proper Section 80(1) notice.
Sub-section (3) saves the suit from dismissal for a defective notice if the plaintiff's identifying details and the cause of action/relief were substantially conveyed and properly delivered.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The urgent-relief carve-out in sub-section (2) is not a free pass — it still requires the Government/officer be heard before any relief is actually granted, and a false claim of urgency risks the plaint being returned.
breakdown.how_to_read: One of the most litigated procedural bars in government litigation — always check notice compliance first; sub-section (3)'s substantial-compliance saving clause is the key defence against a hyper-technical dismissal.

sections.title: Exemption from arrest and personal appearance.
sections.raw_text:
In a suit instituted against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by him in his official capacity—
(a) the defendant shall not be liable to arrest nor his property to attachment otherwise than in execution of a decree, and,
(b) where the Court is satisfied that the defendant cannot absent himself from his duty without detriment to the public service, it shall exempt him from appearing in person.

breakdown.plain_summary: A public officer sued for an official act gets two protections during the suit itself: they can't be arrested or have property attached (except as part of actually executing a decree at the end), and if leaving their post would harm public service, the court must excuse them from appearing in person.
essential_elements: Applies to suits against a public officer for acts purporting to be done in official capacity.
No arrest of the defendant, and no attachment of property, except through execution of an eventual decree.
Personal appearance is excused where the court is satisfied the officer's absence from duty would harm public service.
breakdown.how_to_read: A protective shield for officers during the pendency of the suit — note it does not block ultimate execution of a decree once passed, only pre-decree coercive measures and the appearance requirement.

sections.title: Execution of decree.
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where, in a suit by or against the Government or by or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by him in his official capacity, a decree is passed against the Union of India or a State or, as the case may be, the public officer, such decree shall not be executed except in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2).
(2) Execution shall not be issued on any such decree unless it remains unsatisfied for the period of three months computed from the date of such decree.
(3) The provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) shall apply in relation to an order or award as they apply in relation to a decree, if the order or award—
(a) is passed or made against the Union of India or a State or a public officer in respect of any such act as aforesaid, whether by a Court or by any other authority; and
(b) is capable of being executed under the provisions of this Code or of any other law for the time being in force as if it were a decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: A decree against the Government or a public officer (for an official act) cannot be executed immediately — the Government gets a built-in three-month grace period from the date of the decree to satisfy it voluntarily before coercive execution can begin. The same grace period extends to orders and awards against the Government/officer that are otherwise executable like a decree.
essential_elements: Applies to decrees passed against the Union of India, a State, or a public officer (for an official act) in a suit by or against them.
Execution cannot be issued until the decree has remained unsatisfied for three months from its date.
The same rule extends to orders or awards against the Union/State/public officer that are executable as if they were decrees, whether passed by a court or another authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: A significant timing shield for government litigants — always check whether the three-month window has actually expired before pursuing execution against the Government.

sections.title: When aliens may sue.
sections.raw_text:
Alien enemies residing in India with the permission of the Central Government, and alien friends, may sue in any Court otherwise competent to try the suit, as if they were citizens of India, but alien enemies residing in India without such permission, or residing in a foreign country, shall not sue in any such Court.
Explanation.—Every person residing in a foreign country, the Government of which is at war with India and carrying on business in that country without a licence in that behalf granted by the Central Government, shall, for the purpose of this section, be deemed to be an alien enemy residing in a foreign country.

breakdown.plain_summary: Foreign nationals generally ('alien friends') can sue in Indian courts just like Indian citizens. Nationals of a country at war with India ('alien enemies') can only sue if they reside in India with Central Government permission — an alien enemy abroad, or in India without permission, is barred from suing entirely.
essential_elements: Alien friends may sue as if they were Indian citizens.
Alien enemies residing in India may sue only with the Central Government's permission.
Alien enemies residing in a foreign country, or in India without permission, are barred from suing.
A person trading in an enemy country without a Central Government licence is deemed an alien enemy residing abroad for this purpose.
breakdown.how_to_read: A wartime-oriented access-to-courts rule — rarely invoked outside actual conflict scenarios, but the alien-friend/alien-enemy distinction is the key classification to check.

sections.title: When foreign States may sue.
sections.raw_text: A foreign State may sue in any competent Court: Provided that the object of the suit is to enforce a private right vested in the Ruler of such State or in any officer of such State in his public capacity.

breakdown.plain_summary: A foreign State can bring a suit in an Indian court, but only if the suit is aimed at enforcing a genuinely private right belonging to that State's Ruler or one of its officers acting in their public capacity — not just any claim a foreign State might wish to pursue.
essential_elements: The plaintiff must be a foreign State suing in a court otherwise competent to try the suit.
The suit's object must be to enforce a private right vested in the Ruler of that State, or in an officer of that State acting in a public capacity.
breakdown.how_to_read: Narrower than it first appears — the proviso restricts foreign-State suits to private-right enforcement, so verify the underlying right's character before assuming a foreign State can sue on any claim.

sections.title: Persons specially appointed by Government to prosecute or defend on behalf of foreign Rulers.
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Central Government may, at the request of the Ruler of a foreign State or at the request of any person competent in the opinion of the Central Government to act on behalf of such Ruler, by order, appoint any persons to prosecute or defend any suit on behalf of such Ruler, and any persons so appointed shall be deemed to be the recognized agents by whom appearances, acts and applications under this Code may be made or done on behalf of such Ruler.
(2) An appointment under this section may be made for the purpose of a specified suit or of several specified suits, or for the purpose of all such suits as it may from time to time be necessary to prosecute or defend on behalf of such Ruler.
(3) A person appointed under this section may authorise or appoint any other persons to make appearances and applications and do acts in any such suit or suits as if he were himself a party thereto.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Central Government can formally appoint someone to represent a foreign Ruler in Indian litigation — that appointee becomes the Ruler's official ('recognized') agent for all procedural purposes under the Code, and can even sub-delegate to other people to appear and act in the suit.
essential_elements: Appointment is made by the Central Government, on request of the foreign Ruler or someone the Central Government considers competent to act for the Ruler.
The appointed person becomes the recognized agent through whom appearances, acts, and applications under the Code are made on the Ruler's behalf.
The appointment can cover a single suit, several specified suits, or an open-ended class of suits from time to time.
The appointed agent may further authorise or appoint others to appear and act in the suit(s) as if that sub-delegate were a party.
breakdown.how_to_read: The procedural machinery that makes Section 84's foreign-State suing right practically workable — a foreign Ruler rarely litigates personally; this is how representation is formally established.

sections.title: Suits against foreign Rulers, Ambassadors and Envoys.
sections.raw_text:
(1) No foreign State may be sued in any Court otherwise competent to try the suit except with the consent of the Central Government certified in writing by a Secretary to that Government: Provided that a person may, as a tenant of immovable property, sue without such consent as aforesaid a foreign State from whom he holds or claims to hold the property.
(2) Such consent may be given with respect to a specified suit or to several specified suits or with respect to all suits of any specified class or classes, and may specify, in the case of any suit or class of suits, the Court in which the foreign State may be sued, but it shall not be given, unless it appears to the Central Government that the foreign State—
(a) has instituted a suit in the Court against the person desiring to sue it, or
(b) by itself or another, trades within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, or
(c) is in possession of immovable property situate within those limits and is to be sued with reference to such property or for money charged thereon, or
(d) has expressly or impliedly waived the privilege accorded to it by this section.
(3) Except with the consent of the Central Government, certified in writing by a Secretary to that Government, no decree shall be executed against the property of any foreign State.
(4) The preceding provisions of this section shall apply in relation to—
(a) any Ruler of a foreign State;
(aa) any Ambassador or Envoy of a foreign State;
(b) any High Commissioner of a Commonwealth country; and
(c) any such member of the staff of the foreign State or the staff or retinue of the Ambassador or Envoy of a foreign State or of the High Commissioner of a Commonwealth country as the Central Government may, by general or special order, specify in this behalf, as they apply in relation to a foreign State.
(5) The following persons shall not be arrested under this Code, namely:—
(a) any Ruler of a foreign State;
(b) any Ambassador or Envoy of a foreign State;
(c) any High Commissioner of a Commonwealth country;
(d) any such member of the staff of the foreign State or the staff or retinue of the Ruler, Ambassador or Envoy of a foreign State or of the High Commissioner of a Commonwealth country, as the Central Government may, by general or special order, specify in this behalf.
(6) Where a request is made to the Central Government for the grant of any consent referred to in sub-section (1), the Central Government shall, before refusing to accede to the request in whole or in part, give to the person making the request a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
key_terms: consent conditions for suing foreign State

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 86 codifies sovereign and diplomatic immunity in Indian civil procedure: a foreign State (and, by extension, its Ruler, Ambassadors/Envoys, Commonwealth High Commissioners, and specified staff) generally cannot be sued in India without the Central Government's written consent, and cannot be arrested at all. Consent is granted only in narrow circumstances (the foreign State itself sued first, trades locally, owns local property being sued over, or has waived the privilege) — with a landlord's tenant-suit exception and a right to a hearing before consent is refused.
essential_elements: No suit against a foreign State without the Central Government's written, certified consent, except a tenant may sue the foreign State landlord without consent regarding the tenancy property.
Consent can cover one suit, several suits, or a whole class, and may specify the competent court.
Consent is only to be given where the foreign State itself sued the person first, trades locally, owns local property connected to the suit, or has waived the privilege.
Executing a decree against a foreign State's property likewise requires separate Central Government consent.
The immunity from suit extends to foreign Rulers, Ambassadors/Envoys, Commonwealth High Commissioners, and Central-Government-specified staff/retinue members.
A wider group (Rulers, Ambassadors/Envoys, High Commissioners, and specified staff/retinue) enjoys absolute immunity from arrest under the Code.
Before refusing a consent request, the Central Government must give the requester a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The tenant-suit exception in the proviso to sub-section (1) is the one clear route to sue a foreign State without Government consent.
breakdown.how_to_read: The core sovereign-immunity provision in Indian civil procedure — always check for Central Government consent before proceeding against a foreign State, Ruler, or diplomat; arrest is barred outright regardless of consent.

sections.title: Style of foreign Rulers as parties to suits.
sections.raw_text: The Ruler of a foreign State may sue, and shall be sued, in the name of his State: Provided that in giving the consent referred to in section 86, the Central Government may direct that the Ruler may be sued in the name of an agent or in any other name.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a foreign Ruler is a party to litigation, the cause title normally uses the name of their State rather than their personal name — though the Central Government, when granting consent to sue under Section 86, can direct a different naming convention, such as suing through a named agent.
essential_elements: Default rule: a foreign Ruler sues and is sued in the name of his State.
The Central Government may direct an alternative style (e.g., naming an agent) as part of its Section 86 consent.
breakdown.how_to_read: A drafting-style rule to check when preparing a cause title involving a foreign Ruler — always verify whether the Section 86 consent order specifies a particular naming format.

sections.title: Definitions of "Foreign State" and "Rulers".
sections.raw_text:
(1) In this Part—
(a) "foreign State" means any State outside India which has been recognised by the Central Government; and
(b) "Ruler", in relation to a foreign State, means the person who is for the time being recognized by the Central Government to be the head of that State.
(2) Every Court shall take judicial notice of the fact—
(a) that a State has or has not been recognized by the Central Government;
(b) that a person has or has not been recognized by the Central Government to be the head of a State.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section fixes the meaning of 'foreign State' and 'Ruler' for the whole of Part IV's foreign-State provisions: both terms hinge entirely on Central Government recognition, and courts must simply accept (take judicial notice of) whatever the Central Government has recognized, without needing separate proof.
essential_elements: 'Foreign State' means a State outside India recognized as such by the Central Government.
'Ruler' means the person currently recognized by the Central Government as head of that foreign State.
Courts must take judicial notice of Central Government recognition decisions on both points — no independent evidence is required.
breakdown.how_to_read: A definitional anchor for the whole foreign-State litigation scheme (Sections 83-87B) — recognition is purely an executive, Central Government act that courts accept at face value.

sections.title: Application of sections 85 and 86 to Rulers of former Indian States.
sections.raw_text:
(1) In the case of any suit by or against the Ruler of any former Indian State which is based wholly or in part upon a cause of action which arose before the commencement of the Constitution or any proceeding arising out of such suit, the provisions of section 85 and sub-sections (1) and (3) of section 86 shall apply in relation to such Ruler as they apply in relation to the Ruler of a foreign State.
(2) In this section—
(a) "former Indian State" means any such Indian State as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify for the purposes of this section;
(b) "Commencement of the Constitution" means the 26th day of January, 1950; and
(c) "Ruler", in relation to a former Indian State, has the same meaning as in article 363 of the Constitution.

breakdown.plain_summary: For pre-Independence-era claims (arising before 26 January 1950) against the Ruler of a former princely Indian State, Section 87B extends the same representation-appointment (Section 85) and consent/execution-against-property protections (Section 86(1) and (3)) that apply to foreign-State Rulers.
essential_elements: Applies to suits (or proceedings arising from them) against a Ruler of a former Indian State, where the cause of action arose wholly or partly before 26 January 1950.
Extends Section 85 (appointment of recognized agents) and Section 86(1) and (3) (consent to sue / consent to execute against property) to such Rulers as if they were foreign-State Rulers.
"Former Indian State" is limited to States the Central Government has specifically notified for this purpose.
"Ruler" carries the meaning given in Article 363 of the Constitution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Only Section 86 sub-sections (1) and (3) are extended, not the full section — the trading/local-property consent conditions in sub-section (2) are not incorporated by this cross-reference.
breakdown.how_to_read: A historical transitional provision, now of narrowing relevance given its pre-1950 cause-of-action requirement, but still material in long-pending or property-succession litigation tracing back to princely-State-era claims.

sections.title: Where interpleader suit may be instituted.
sections.raw_text: Where two or more persons claim adversely to one another the same debts, sum of money or other property, movable or immovable, from another person, who claims no interest therein other than for charges or costs and who is ready to pay or deliver it to the rightful claimant, such other person may institute a suit of interpleader against all the claimants for the purpose of obtaining a decision as to the person to whom the payment or delivery shall be made and of obtaining indemnity for himself: Provided that where any suit is pending in which the rights of all parties can properly be decided, no such suit of interpleader shall be instituted.

breakdown.plain_summary: An interpleader suit lets a neutral stakeholder — someone holding money or property that two or more rival claimants are fighting over, and who has no personal stake beyond costs — ask the court to decide who the rightful claimant actually is, so the stakeholder can safely hand it over and be done with the dispute.
essential_elements: Two or more persons must claim, adversely to each other, the same debt, sum, or property from a third party.
That third party (the stakeholder) must claim no interest in the subject-matter beyond charges or costs, and must be ready to hand it to whoever is rightfully entitled.
The stakeholder sues all the rival claimants together, seeking a decision on entitlement and indemnity for themselves.
Barred if a suit is already pending in which the rights of all parties can properly be decided.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Not available where existing litigation already covers the same ground between all the relevant parties.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read with Order XXXV for the detailed interpleader-suit procedure; the plaintiff's defining feature is genuine neutrality — no real stake in who wins beyond wanting to safely discharge the obligation.

sections.title: Settlement of disputes outside the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 89 institutionalizes alternative dispute resolution within civil litigation: if the court senses a settlement is possible, it drafts settlement terms, gets the parties' reactions, refines them, and then sends the dispute off to one of four tracks — arbitration, conciliation, Lok Adalat/judicial settlement, or mediation — each governed by its own specialized statute once referred.
essential_elements: Trigger: the court perceives elements of an acceptable settlement.
Process: the court formulates settlement terms, invites party observations, and may reformulate before referring the dispute out.
Four referral tracks are available: arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement (including Lok Adalat), or mediation.
Arbitration/conciliation references are governed by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 as if the parties had referred the matter under that Act.
Lok Adalat references follow Section 20(1) of the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987, with that Act applying fully.
Judicial settlement references go to a suitable institution or person, deemed a Lok Adalat, again attracting the full Legal Services Authority Act, 1987 framework.
Mediation references require the court itself to work towards effecting a compromise following prescribed procedure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a court-driven referral mechanism triggered by the court's own assessment, though in practice courts commonly invite party consent before referring.
breakdown.how_to_read: The gateway provision for court-referred ADR — a landmark modernization of the Code; practitioners should be alert to which of the four tracks is chosen, since each pulls in a distinct external statutory regime.

sections.title: Power to state case for opinion of Court.
sections.raw_text: Where any person agree in writing to state a case for the opinion of the Court, then the Court shall try and determine the same in the manner prescribed.

breakdown.plain_summary: Parties who agree in writing can jointly place an agreed statement of facts (a 'special case') before the court simply to get its opinion/ruling on the legal question involved, using the prescribed procedure, without a full adversarial trial of disputed facts.
essential_elements: Requires a written agreement between the parties to state a case for the court's opinion.
The court then tries and determines the stated case following the manner prescribed (Order XXXVI).
breakdown.how_to_read: A streamlined, consent-based route to obtain judicial clarity on a legal question where the facts are not really in dispute — see Order XXXVI for the procedural mechanics of framing and trying a special case.

sections.title: Public nuisances and other wrongful acts affecting the public
sections.raw_text:
(1) In the case of a public nuisance or other wrongful act affecting, or likely to affect, the public, a suit for a declaration and injunction or for such other relief as may be appropriate in the circumstances of the case, may be instituted,—
(a) by the Advocate-General, or
(b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons by reason of such public nuisance or other wrongful act.
(2) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any right of suit which may exist independently of its provisions.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets a suit be filed to stop a public nuisance or other wrongful act harming the public at large, even though no individual plaintiff has suffered any special, personal damage beyond what the general public suffers. Ordinarily a plaintiff must show a personal injury to have standing to sue; Section 91 creates a statutory exception for public wrongs.
essential_elements: The wrong complained of must be a 'public nuisance' or 'other wrongful act' that affects, or is likely to affect, the public generally, not just the plaintiff.
The suit may be brought by the Advocate-General on his own authority, without needing the Court's leave.
Alternatively, it may be brought by two or more private persons, but only with the leave (permission) of the Court obtained before or at the institution of the suit.
The relief claimed is typically a declaration and an injunction, or such other relief as the circumstances warrant — not damages to the plaintiffs personally.
No proof of special damage to the plaintiffs is required — this is the section's core departure from ordinary civil suit standing.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (2) preserves any independent right of suit that already exists outside Section 91 — for instance, a person who has actually suffered special damage beyond the general public can still sue in their own right without needing Section 91 or the Court's leave.
Where two or more persons sue under clause (b) without having first obtained the leave of the Court, the suit is liable to be dismissed for want of the mandatory pre-condition.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the general public-interest-litigation gateway of the Code, predating and complementing the modern PIL jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court under Articles 226 and 32 of the Constitution. It is most often invoked for obstruction of public roads, encroachment on public land, and pollution or other environmental wrongs affecting a community.

sections.title: Public charities

breakdown.plain_summary: This section provides the special procedural gateway for suits about public charitable or religious trusts — removing or appointing trustees, settling a 'scheme' for administering the trust, or redirecting trust property to a new purpose when the original purpose has failed or become impossible (the cy pres doctrine in sub-section (3)). Like Section 91, it departs from ordinary suit rules because the beneficiaries of a public trust are the public at large, not identifiable individuals.
essential_elements: There must be an alleged breach of an express or constructive trust created for public purposes of a charitable or religious nature, or a need for the Court's directions in administering such a trust.
The suit may be brought by the Advocate-General, or by two or more persons who have an interest in the trust and have obtained the Court's leave.

It must be filed in the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction (or another Court empowered by the State Government) within whose local limits the trust property, wholly or partly, is situated.

The suit seeks one or more of the specific reliefs listed in clauses (a) to (h) — removal/appointment of trustees, vesting of property, accounts, allocation of trust property among objects, authorizing sale/lease/mortgage/exchange, settling a scheme, or other appropriate relief.

Under sub-section (3), the cy pres power to redirect trust property to a new but kindred purpose can only be exercised where one of the five specific circumstances in clauses (a) to (e) is shown to exist.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (2) makes Section 92 procedure mandatory (subject to the Religious Endowments Act, 1863 or corresponding State law) for any suit claiming the specific reliefs listed in sub-section (1) in respect of a public trust — a suit seeking those reliefs cannot bypass Section 92 by being framed as an ordinary suit.

Section 92 does not apply to suits asserting a purely private or individual right (such as a beneficiary's individual share) or to suits against persons who are strangers to the trust; it is confined to suits for the specific administrative reliefs concerning the trust as a whole.

A suit under this section is not necessarily contentious — it may proceed even where there is no real dispute, since its purpose can be simply to obtain the Court's directions for proper administration.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the standard route for disputes over temples, mosques, churches, charitable endowments, and public trusts generally — practitioners must check at the threshold whether the plaintiff has obtained the Court's leave under sub-section (1) before institution, since want of leave is a common ground for dismissal or rejection.

sections.title: Exercise of powers of Advocate-General outside presidency-towns
sections.raw_text: The powers conferred by sections 91 and 92 on the Advocate-General may, outside the presidency-towns, be, with the previous sanction of the State Government, exercised also by the Collector or by such officer as the State Government may appoint in this behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary: Outside the old presidency-towns (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras), the Advocate-General's powers to institute suits under Sections 91 (public nuisance) and 92 (public charities) can also be exercised by the Collector of the district, or by another officer the State Government appoints for the purpose — with the State Government's prior sanction.
essential_elements: Applies only outside the presidency-towns.
The State Government's previous sanction is required before the Collector or appointed officer can exercise the Advocate-General's Section 91/92 powers.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical delegation provision — in mofussil (non-presidency) areas, litigants and practitioners should check whether the Collector or a State-appointed officer, rather than the Advocate-General personally, is the one authorized to sue or consent under Sections 91 and 92.

sections.title: Supplemental proceedings

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 94 is the umbrella enabling provision for the Court's interim/interlocutory powers during the pendency of a suit — arrest before judgment, security for production of property, temporary injunctions, appointment of receivers, and other just-and-convenient interlocutory orders — all aimed at preventing a defendant from defeating the ultimate relief before the suit is decided. The actual detailed machinery for each of these powers is worked out in the corresponding Orders of the First Schedule (e.g., Order XXXVIII for arrest/attachment before judgment, Order XXXIX for temporary injunctions, Order XL for receivers).
essential_elements: The overarching purpose stated in the section itself is to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated — this is the touchstone against which every exercise of these powers is tested.

The power under each clause is exercisable only 'if it is so prescribed' — meaning the specific procedural conditions in the relevant Order/Rule of the First Schedule must be satisfied; Section 94 alone does not supply the procedure.
Clause (a): arrest and require security for appearance, with civil imprisonment on default.
Clause (b): security to produce property, or attachment of property.
Clause (c): temporary injunctions, with civil imprisonment and attachment/sale of property on disobedience.
Clause (d): appointment of a receiver, enforceable by attachment and sale of the receiver's own property for default.
Clause (e): a residuary power for any other interlocutory order the Court considers just and convenient.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 94 is procedural machinery, not a source of independent substantive right — a party must bring itself within the specific requirements of the corresponding Order (e.g., Order XXXVIII Rule 5 for attachment before judgment) before the Court will exercise the power.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 94 is the doctrinal anchor cited alongside the specific Order/Rule whenever an interim application (arrest before judgment, attachment before judgment, temporary injunction, or receiver) is moved — practitioners plead the substantive Order/Rule for the detailed test, and cite Section 94 for the Court's underlying power and purpose.

sections.title: Compensation for obtaining arrest, attachment or injunction on insufficient grounds
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where, in any suit in which an arrest or attachment has been effected or a temporary injunction granted under the last preceding section,—
(a) it appears to the Court that such arrest, attachment or injunction was applied for on insufficient grounds, or
(b) the suit of the plaintiff fails and it appears to the Court that there was no reasonable or probable grounds for instituting the same,
the defendant may apply to the Court, and the Court may, upon such application, award against the plaintiff by its order such amount not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, as it deems a reasonable compensation to the defendant for the expense or injury (including injury to reputation) caused to him:
Provided that a Court shall not award, under this section an amount exceeding the limits of its pecuniary jurisdiction.
(2) An order determining any such application shall bar any suit for compensation in respect of such arrest, attachment or injunction.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section is a built-in check on the interim powers of Section 94 — if a plaintiff obtains an arrest, attachment, or temporary injunction against a defendant on insufficient grounds, or the plaintiff's whole suit later fails for want of reasonable grounds, the defendant can apply in that very suit for compensation up to fifty thousand rupees, capped further by the Court's own pecuniary jurisdiction limit.
essential_elements: There must have been an arrest, attachment, or temporary injunction actually granted under Section 94 in the suit.

Either: (a) the Court finds the application for that interim relief was made on insufficient grounds, or (b) the plaintiff's suit ultimately fails and there was no reasonable or probable ground for instituting it.
The defendant must make a specific application to the Court for compensation.
The maximum compensation is fifty thousand rupees, further capped at the Court's own pecuniary jurisdiction limit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: An order determining a Section 95 compensation application operates as a complete bar to any separate suit for compensation (e.g., a suit for malicious prosecution/wrongful attachment) in respect of the same arrest, attachment, or injunction — the defendant cannot pursue both remedies.
breakdown.how_to_read: A defendant who has been arrested, had property attached, or been restrained by an injunction that later proves baseless should move a Section 95 application in the same suit rather than filing a fresh suit for damages — filing both, or filing a fresh suit after a Section 95 order, is barred by sub-section (2).

sections.title: Appeal from original decree
sections.raw_text:
(1) Save where otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, an appeal shall lie from every decree passed by any Court exercising original jurisdiction the Court authorized to hear appeals from the decisions of such Court.
(2) An appeal may lie from an original decree passed ex parte.
(3) No appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the Court with the consent of parties.
(4) No appeal shall lie, except on a question of law, from a decree in any suit of the nature cognisable by Courts of Small Causes, when the amount or value of the subject-matter of the original suit does not exceed ten thousand rupees.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the foundational provision creating the general right of first appeal against every decree passed by a trial court exercising original jurisdiction, unless the Code or some other law expressly bars it. It also carves out three important exceptions/clarifications: an ex parte decree can still be appealed (sub-section 2), a decree passed with the parties' consent cannot be appealed at all (sub-section 3), and small-cause-nature suits below the prescribed value can only be appealed on a question of law (sub-section 4).
essential_elements: A decree must have been passed by a Court exercising original (trial-level) jurisdiction.
The appeal lies to the Court authorized by law to hear appeals from that Court's decisions.
The right of appeal exists unless expressly barred by the Code itself or by any other law in force.
Sub-section (2) confirms even an ex parte decree (passed in the defendant's absence) is appealable — the aggrieved defendant is not limited to only an application to set aside the ex parte decree.
Sub-section (3) bars appeal entirely where the decree was passed by consent of the parties, since a consenting party cannot later claim to be aggrieved by what it agreed to.
Sub-section (4) restricts appeals from decrees in small-cause-nature suits valued at ten thousand rupees or less to only a 'question of law', not questions of fact.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The right of first appeal under Section 96 is a substantive right (not merely procedural), vesting at the date the suit is instituted — a subsequent amendment restricting appealability does not retrospectively take away an already-accrued right of appeal, per settled Supreme Court jurisprudence on the nature of appellate rights.

A consent decree can still be challenged, but not by way of a Section 96 appeal — the aggrieved party's remedy is a suit or application to set aside the decree on grounds such as fraud, lack of genuine consent, or absence of jurisdiction to record the compromise.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 96 is the default entry point for challenging any trial-court decree; before drafting a memorandum of appeal, check whether the decree falls into one of the sub-section (3)/(4) restrictions (consent decree, or small-value small-cause suit) which would either bar the appeal altogether or confine it strictly to a question of law.

sections.title: Appeal from final decree where no appeal from preliminary decree
sections.raw_text: Where any party aggrieved by a preliminary decree passed after the commencement of this Code does not appeal from such decree, he shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: In suits (such as partition or accounts suits) that proceed in two decree-stages — a preliminary decree settling rights, followed later by a final decree implementing those rights — a party who fails to appeal the preliminary decree cannot later reopen or challenge its correctness when appealing the final decree. The preliminary decree becomes conclusive as between the parties once the appeal period lapses without an appeal.
essential_elements: There must be a preliminary decree passed after the commencement of the Code (1908), followed later by a final decree in the same suit.
The aggrieved party did not file any appeal against the preliminary decree within the limitation period.
That party is then barred from questioning the correctness of the preliminary decree's findings in a later appeal against the final decree.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar applies only to the correctness of matters actually decided by the preliminary decree — issues not decided at the preliminary stage, or arising only at the final-decree stage, remain open to appeal.
breakdown.how_to_read: A critical timing trap for practitioners handling multi-stage suits (partition, accounts, pre-emption): any grievance against the preliminary decree's findings on shares, liability, or entitlement must be appealed immediately — waiting to challenge it via the final-decree appeal is fatal under Section 97.

sections.title: Decision where appeal heard by two or more Judges
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where an appeal is heard by a Bench of two or more Judges, the appeal shall be decided in accordance with the opinion of such Judges or of the majority (if any) of such Judges.
(2) Where there is no such majority which concurs in a judgment varying or reversing the decree appealed from, such decree shall be confirmed:
Provided that where the Bench hearing the appeal is composed of two or other even number of Judges belonging to a Court consisting of more Judges than those constituting the Bench and the Judges composing the Bench differ in opinion on a point of law, they may state the point of law upon which they differ and the appeal shall then be heard upon that point only by one or more of the other Judges, and such point shall be decided according to the opinion of the majority (if any) of the Judges who have heard the appeal, including those who first heard it.
(3) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to alter or otherwise affect any provision of the letters to patent of any High Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section governs how a Division Bench (or larger Bench) of an appellate court resolves a difference of opinion among its Judges. If there is a majority view, that prevails. If the Bench splits evenly with no majority to vary or reverse, the decree under appeal stands confirmed by default. But where the split is specifically on a point of law, the Bench can instead refer just that point of law to one or more additional Judges for a majority resolution — this is the statutory root of the 'reference to a larger/third Judge' procedure familiar in High Court practice.
essential_elements: Applies where an appeal is heard by a Bench of two or more Judges.
The appeal is decided according to the opinion of the Judges, or the majority view if they differ.
If no majority exists to vary or reverse the decree, the decree appealed from stands confirmed by operation of sub-section (2).

The proviso allows an even-numbered Bench differing specifically on a point of law to state that point and refer it to one or more other Judges of the same Court, with the ultimate result governed by the majority of all Judges who heard the appeal (including the original two).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (3) preserves the special Letters Patent provisions of chartered High Courts governing reference in case of difference of opinion, which continue to operate alongside (not in place of) Section 98.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the provision practitioners cite when a Division Bench delivers a split verdict — knowing whether the disagreement is purely on a point of law (triggering the proviso's reference mechanism) or more broadly on the decree's correctness (triggering the default-confirmation rule of sub-section (2)) determines the next procedural step.

sections.title: No decree to be reversed or modified for error or irregularity not affecting merits or jurisdiction
sections.raw_text:
No decree shall be reversed or substantially varied, nor shall any case be remanded, in appeal on account of any misjoinder or non-joinder of parties or causes of action or any error, defect or irregularity in any proceedings in the suit, not affecting the merits of the case or the jurisdiction of the Court:
Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to non-joinder of a necessary party.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section embodies the principle that appellate courts should not overturn substantially correct decrees merely because of technical, non-prejudicial defects in the proceedings below — such as a wrong joinder of parties or causes of action, or a procedural irregularity — unless that defect actually affected the merits of the case or the trial court's jurisdiction. The one hard exception is the non-joinder of a truly 'necessary party' (one without whom no effective decree can be passed), which remains fatal even under this otherwise forgiving rule.
essential_elements: The defect complained of on appeal must be a misjoinder or non-joinder of parties/causes of action, or some other error, defect, or irregularity in the suit proceedings.

That defect must not have affected the merits of the case or the jurisdiction of the trial Court — if it did, Section 99 provides no protection and the decree remains liable to be reversed, varied, or remanded.
Where the conditions are met, the appellate court is barred from reversing, substantially varying, or remanding the case purely on account of such a harmless defect.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso expressly excludes non-joinder of a necessary party from this protective rule — failure to implead a necessary party remains a ground on which a decree can be reversed or the suit dismissed, because no binding decree can effectively be passed in that party's absence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 99 is the standard shield an appellant-respondent invokes to resist a reversal sought purely on a technical/procedural ground; conversely, an appellant seeking reversal on a joinder defect must specifically show either prejudice to the merits, want of jurisdiction, or that the omitted party was a genuinely necessary (not merely proper) party.

sections.title: No order under section 47 to be reversed or modified unless decision of the case is prejudicially affected
sections.raw_text: Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of section 99, no order under section 47 shall be reversed or substantially varied, on account of any error, defect or irregularity in any proceeding relating to such order, unless such error, defect or irregularity has prejudicially affected the decision of the case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section extends the same 'no reversal for harmless error' philosophy of Section 99 specifically to orders passed under Section 47 (questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree, decided by the executing court). Such an order cannot be reversed or substantially varied on appeal for a procedural defect unless that defect actually prejudiced the decision of the case.
essential_elements: The order under challenge must be one passed under Section 47 (execution, discharge, or satisfaction questions between the parties to the decree).
There must be some error, defect, or irregularity in the proceeding relating to that order.
The order cannot be reversed or substantially varied unless the error, defect, or irregularity has prejudicially affected the decision of the case — mere technical irregularity is not enough.
breakdown.how_to_read: Invoked specifically in appeals from execution-related orders decided under Section 47 — the appellant carries the burden of demonstrating actual prejudice to the outcome, not just a procedural slip in the execution proceedings.

sections.title: Second appeal
sections.raw_text:
(1) Save as otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, an appeal shall lie to the High Court from every decree passed in appeal by any Court subordinate to the High Court, if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law.
(2) An appeal may lie under this section from an appellate decree passed ex parte.
(3) In an appeal under this section, the memorandum of appeal shall precisely state the substantial question of law involved in the appeal.
(4) Where the High Court is satisfied that a substantial question of law is involved in any case, it shall formulate that question.
(5) The appeal shall be heard on the question so formulated and the respondent shall, at the hearing of the appeal, be allowed to argue that the case does not involve such question:
Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall be deemed to take away or abridge the power of the Court to hear, for reasons to be recorded, the appeal on any other substantial question of law, not formulated by it, if it is satisfied that the case involves such question.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 100 is the tightly-gated 'second appeal' provision — a further appeal to the High Court against a decree already passed in a first appeal, available only where the case involves a 'substantial question of law', not merely a disputed question of fact or a routine misapplication of settled law. The memorandum of appeal must precisely state that question, the High Court must formally 'formulate' it before final hearing, and the appeal proceeds on that formulated question alone (subject to a limited power to consider an unformulated additional substantial question of law).
essential_elements: There must be a decree passed in (first) appeal by a Court subordinate to the High Court.
The High Court must be satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law — a threshold gate, not automatic like Section 96's first-appeal right.
The memorandum of appeal must precisely state the substantial question of law relied upon (sub-section 3) — a defectively framed memorandum risks summary dismissal.
The High Court must formulate the substantial question(s) of law at the admission stage (sub-section 4); the appeal is thereafter heard confined to that formulated question (sub-section 5).
The respondent retains the right, at final hearing, to argue that the case does not actually involve the formulated question.

The proviso to sub-section (5) allows the High Court, for recorded reasons, to hear the appeal on an additional substantial question of law it did not originally formulate, if satisfied the case involves it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A pure question of fact, or a mixed question that does not rise to a 'substantial' question of law, cannot sustain a second appeal — concurrent findings of fact by the trial and first-appellate courts are ordinarily not reopened in second appeal.

'Substantial' means the question must be of general public importance, or must directly and substantially affect the rights of the parties, and must not already be settled by binding precedent — a question already conclusively answered by a Supreme Court ruling is not 'substantial' in this sense.

State Amendment (Kerala): adds a further specific ground — where the first-appellate court's finding on a material question of fact conflicts with the finding of the trial court on the same question — as itself capable of constituting a substantial question of law under Kerala's local amendment.
breakdown.how_to_read: The single most heavily litigated procedural threshold in CPC appellate practice: drafting the memorandum of appeal to precisely and persuasively frame a genuine 'substantial question of law' (not a disguised question of fact) is often outcome-determinative at the admission stage, since a large proportion of second appeals are dismissed in limine for failing this threshold.

sections.title: No further appeal in certain cases
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything contained in any Letters Patent for any High Court or in any instrument having the force of law or in any other law for the time being in force, where any appeal from an original or appellate decree or order is heard and decided by a Single Judge of a High Court, no further appeal shall lie from the judgment and decree of such Single Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section abolishes the traditional 'Letters Patent Appeal' (an intra-High-Court appeal from a Single Judge to a Division Bench of the same High Court) in respect of any appeal from an original or appellate decree/order that was heard and decided by a Single Judge — the Single Judge's decision is final within the High Court, notwithstanding any contrary provision in the High Court's Letters Patent or other law.
essential_elements: The non-obstante opening overrides any Letters Patent provision or other law that would otherwise allow a further intra-Court appeal.
Applies where an appeal (from an original or appellate decree or order) was heard and decided by a Single Judge of a High Court.
The consequence is an absolute bar: no further appeal lies from that Single Judge's judgment and decree within the High Court system.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar is confined to appeals decided by a Single Judge; it does not affect the separate question of a further appeal (e.g., to the Supreme Court under Section 109 or Article 136) from a decision of a Division Bench.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners in High Courts that traditionally had Letters Patent Appeal practice must check Section 100A first before assuming an LPA lies from a Single Judge's decision in a first or second appeal — this section forecloses that route.

sections.title: Second appeal on no other grounds
sections.raw_text: No second appeal shall lie except on the ground mentioned in section 100.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a short reinforcing provision making clear that a substantial question of law under Section 100 is the only permissible ground for a second appeal — no other ground (such as a pure factual grievance) can independently sustain one.
essential_elements: A second appeal can be founded on no ground other than a substantial question of law as contemplated by Section 100.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cited alongside Section 100 to rebuff attempts to argue a second appeal purely on facts or equity without a properly formulated substantial question of law.

sections.title: No second appeal in certain cases
sections.raw_text: No second appeal shall lie from any decree, when the subject matter of the original suit is for recovery of money not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section imposes an absolute pecuniary bar on second appeals in money suits: if the original suit was for recovery of money and the subject-matter did not exceed twenty-five thousand rupees, no second appeal lies at all — regardless of whether a substantial question of law might otherwise exist under Section 100.
essential_elements: The original suit must have been for recovery of money (a money suit, not a suit for other reliefs like possession or injunction).
The subject-matter (amount claimed) must not exceed twenty-five thousand rupees.
Where both conditions are met, the bar is absolute — no second appeal lies, even on a substantial question of law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar applies specifically to money suits; suits for other reliefs (even if incidentally involving a small money component) are not automatically barred merely because a money element is below the threshold.
breakdown.how_to_read: A quick pecuniary-value check practitioners should run before advising a client on a second appeal in a money-recovery matter — below the threshold, the only available remedies are (where applicable) a revision or a constitutional writ, not a Section 100 second appeal.

sections.title: Power of High Court to determine issue of fact
sections.raw_text:
In any second appeal, the High Court may, if the evidence on the record is sufficient, determine any issue necessary for the disposal of the appeal,—
(a) which has not been determined by the lower Appellate Court or both by the Court of first instance and the lower Appellate Court, or
(b) which has been wrongly determined by such Court or Courts by reason of a decision on such question of law as is referred to in section 100.
key_terms: issue of fact in second appeal
