'Court which passed the decree or order' extends to the Court of first instance (Explanation (a)) or, where that Court no longer has jurisdiction, whichever Court would now have jurisdiction to try the suit (Explanation (b))
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (2) bars a separate suit for relief that could be obtained by application under sub-section (1) — restitution must ordinarily be sought by application, not fresh litigation
The restitution must be 'properly consequential' on the variation/reversal — it cannot be used to claim relief unconnected to the undone part of the decree
Restitution restores the position only 'so far as may be' — perfect restoration is not always achievable (e.g., where property has since been transferred to a bona fide third party)
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 144 is a high-value practitioner tool: whenever a client's decree is reversed or modified on appeal, immediately consider filing a restitution application in the original (trial) Court rather than a fresh suit — Section 144(2)'s bar means a fresh suit for the same relief risks outright dismissal; also invoke it proactively to recover money, possession, or property that changed hands under an eventually-overturned decree, including claims for mesne profits and interest for the period of wrongful enjoyment.

sections.title: Enforcement of liability of surety
sections.raw_text: Where any person has furnished security or given a guarantee— (a) for the performance of any decree or any part thereof, or (b) for the restitution of any property taken in execution of a decree, or (c) for the payment of any money, or for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person, under an order of the Court in any suit or in any proceeding consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed— (i) in the case of a security or guarantee for the performance of a decree or part thereof, or for the restitution of property, against such person, to the extent to which he has rendered himself personally liable, in the manner herein provided for the execution of decrees, and such person shall, for the purposes of appeal, be deemed a party within the meaning of section 47; (ii) in the case of a security for the payment of money or for the fulfilment of a condition, by the Court holding that any such person, so far as he has rendered himself personally liable, is liable to satisfy the claim.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 145 provides a simplified, direct route to enforce the obligations of a surety — someone who has furnished security or given a personal guarantee in connection with civil litigation, whether to guarantee that a decree will be performed, that property taken in execution will be restored, or that money will be paid/a condition fulfilled under a Court order. Rather than requiring a fresh suit against the surety to establish and enforce that liability, Section 145 allows the decree or order itself to be executed directly against the surety, to the extent of the personal liability the surety has undertaken, using the ordinary decree-execution machinery. For purposes of appeal, such a surety is treated as a 'party' within the meaning of Section 47 (questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree), giving the surety the same procedural standing as a party to the suit when it comes to resisting or appealing the execution against them.
essential_elements: A person has furnished security or given a guarantee — for performance of a decree/part of it, for restitution of property taken in execution, or for payment of money/fulfilment of a condition under a Court order
That guarantee arises in connection with a suit or a proceeding consequent on it
The decree or order can then be executed directly against the surety, to the extent of their personal liability, using ordinary decree-execution procedure
The surety is deemed a party within the meaning of Section 47 for purposes of appeal
exceptions_and_qualifications: Liability is enforceable only 'to the extent' the surety has rendered himself personally liable — not beyond the scope of the guarantee actually given
This is a summary execution mechanism, avoiding the need for a fresh suit against the surety, but it does not create liability beyond what the surety agreed to
breakdown.how_to_read: A key practitioner tool when a decree-holder needs to realize a decree from a surety (e.g., a bank guarantee furnished for stay of execution, or personal security given for restitution of attached property) — proceed by execution application against the surety under Section 145 rather than filing a fresh suit, and remember the surety has full Section 47 party-status to contest the execution or appeal an adverse order.

sections.title: Proceedings by or against representatives
sections.raw_text: Save as otherwise provided by this Code or by any law for the time being in force, where any proceeding may be taken or application made by or against any person, then the proceeding may be taken or the application may be made by or against any person claiming under him.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 146 is a broad enabling provision allowing continuity of civil proceedings across a change in the identity of the person entitled or liable. Where the Code (or any other law) permits some proceeding to be taken, or an application to be made, by or against a particular person, Section 146 extends that same permission to any other person who 'claims under' that original person — that is, someone who derives their right or liability through them, such as a legal heir, assignee, transferee, or successor-in-interest. This avoids technical dead-ends where a right created by or against one person would otherwise be unusable by or against someone who has since stepped into that person's shoes.
essential_elements: A proceeding may be taken, or an application made, by or against a given person under the Code or another law
Another person claims under that original person (e.g., as heir, assignee, or successor-in-interest)
That derivative claimant may equally take the proceeding or make the application, or have it taken/made against them
Subject to any contrary provision made elsewhere in the Code or in another law
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies only 'save as otherwise provided' — a specific provision elsewhere in the Code or another statute displacing this general rule prevails
The claimant must genuinely be someone 'claiming under' the original person — i.e., holding a derivative title or interest, not a wholly unconnected third party
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 146 is regularly invoked to justify legal representatives, assignees, or transferees pursuing or resisting execution proceedings, appeals, or other applications originally available to/against the person they succeed — useful where procedural rules speak only of 'the plaintiff', 'the decree-holder', or 'the judgment-debtor' without expressly naming successors.

sections.title: Consent or agreement by persons under disability
sections.raw_text: Where, in any provision of this Code, it is provided that any act may be done by any party to a suit with the consent of the Court, the Court shall, in respect of a party who is under any disability, accord or withhold consent after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, or in accordance with the procedure prescribed by rules made in this behalf by the High Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: Certain provisions of the Code let a party do something only 'with the consent of the Court' — for example, entering into a compromise or adjustment of a suit. Section 147 addresses the special situation where the party in question is under a legal disability (such as a minor or a person of unsound mind, who cannot validly consent for themselves). In such cases, the Court itself must decide whether to grant or withhold the necessary consent on the disabled party's behalf, doing so only after making whatever inquiry it considers appropriate, or by following a procedure the High Court has separately prescribed by rules. This is a protective safeguard ensuring vulnerable litigants aren't bound by consequential acts (like compromises) taken without genuine, informed authorization.
essential_elements: A Code provision allows a party to do some act 'with the consent of the Court'
The party concerned is under a legal disability
The Court itself must decide whether to accord or withhold that consent on the disabled party's behalf
This is done after such inquiry as the Court thinks fit, or per High Court-prescribed procedure
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies only where the underlying provision already requires 'the consent of the Court' as a condition — it does not create a fresh consent requirement where none otherwise exists
The precise inquiry standard is left to the Court's discretion or to specific High Court rules
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Order XXXII (suits by or against minors and persons of unsound mind) — whenever a compromise or other consent-dependent act is proposed on behalf of a minor or disabled party (e.g., under Order XXIII Rule 3's compromise provisions), Section 147 requires the Court's own considered sanction, not a bare next-friend/guardian signature, before it can bind that party.

sections.title: Enlargement of time
sections.raw_text: Where any period is fixed or granted by the Court for the doing of any act prescribed or allowed by this Code, the Court may, in its discretion, from time to time, enlarge such period, [not exceeding thirty days in total,] even though the period originally fixed or granted may have expired.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 148 gives Courts a general discretionary power to extend time-limits they themselves have fixed or granted for doing something under the Code — even after the originally fixed period has already run out. This prevents litigants from being fatally prejudiced by minor delays where the time-limit in question is one the Court itself set (as opposed to a limitation period fixed directly by statute, such as under the Limitation Act, which this section cannot override). The extension is capped (following the 1976 amendment) at a total of thirty days beyond what was originally granted, and remains entirely at the Court's discretion — it is not a right the party can claim automatically.
essential_elements: A period has been fixed or granted by the Court (not by the Code or another statute directly) for doing some act prescribed or allowed by the Code
The Court may enlarge that period in its discretion, from time to time
The enlargement may be granted even after the originally fixed period has already expired
The total enlargement is capped at thirty days
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies only to Court-fixed/granted periods, not statutory limitation periods (e.g., under the Limitation Act, 1963) which the Court has no power to extend under this section
The power is discretionary, not automatic — the party must show sufficient cause or otherwise persuade the Court to exercise its discretion
The cumulative extension cannot exceed thirty days
breakdown.how_to_read: A frequently invoked provision in interlocutory practice — used to seek extension of time to file a written statement, comply with an order, or take a procedural step the Court had earlier timed; always distinguish it clearly from Section 5 of the Limitation Act (condonation of delay for statutory limitation periods), which is a separate and distinct power.

sections.title: Right to lodge a caveat
sections.raw_text: (1) Where an application is expected to be made, or has been made, in a suit or proceeding instituted, or about to be instituted, in a Court, any person claiming a right to appear before the Court on the hearing of such application may lodge a caveat in respect thereof. (2) Where a caveat has been lodged under sub-section (1), the person by whom the caveat has been lodged (hereinafter referred to as the caveator) shall serve a notice of the caveat by registered post, acknowledgment due, on the person by whom the application has been, or is expected to be, made. (3) Where, after a caveat has been lodged under sub-section (1), any application is filed in any suit or proceeding, the Court shall serve a notice of the application on the caveator. (4) Where a notice of any caveat has been served on the applicant, he shall forthwith furnish the caveator, at the caveator's expense, with a copy of the application made by him and also with copies of any paper or document which has been, or may be, filed by him in support of the application. (5) Where a caveat has been lodged under sub-section (1), such caveat shall not remain in force after the expiry of ninety days from the date on which it was lodged unless the application referred to in sub-section (1) has been made before the expiry of the said period.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 148A protects a person's right to be heard before an ex parte order is made against their interest, in a suit or proceeding they anticipate may be filed or is about to be filed against them. By lodging a 'caveat' — literally, a warning — with the Court, that person (the caveator) ensures that if the anticipated application is actually filed, the Court must notify them before deciding it, rather than passing an order (such as an ex parte interim injunction) without giving them a chance to be heard. The caveator must serve notice of the caveat by registered post with acknowledgment due on the person expected to file the application. If that application is then filed, the Court is obliged to notify the caveator, and the applicant must in turn (at the caveator's own expense) furnish the caveator copies of the application and any supporting papers or documents — putting the caveator in a position to appear and be heard. A caveat is not indefinitely effective: it lapses automatically ninety days after being lodged unless the anticipated application is actually filed within that window.
essential_elements: A person expects an application to be made (or one has already been made) in a suit or proceeding instituted or about to be instituted
That person claims a right to appear before the Court when that application is heard
They lodge a caveat and serve notice of it by registered post, acknowledgment due, on the person expected to make the application

If the application is then filed, the Court must serve notice of it on the caveator, and the applicant must furnish the caveator with copies of the application and supporting papers, at the caveator's expense
The caveat lapses automatically after ninety days unless the application is filed within that period
exceptions_and_qualifications: The caveat protects only the caveator's right to notice and hearing on the specific anticipated application — it does not itself block the filing or institution of the suit/proceeding
Validity is strictly time-bound: ninety days from lodging, with no provision here for extension or renewal beyond re-lodging afresh
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 148A is an essential pre-emptive tool for a prospective defendant who anticipates an ex parte interim application (most commonly an ex parte temporary injunction) being sought against them — lodging a caveat the moment litigation is anticipated forces the Court to hear the caveator before granting any such ex parte relief, and practitioners should calendar the ninety-day expiry to re-lodge if the anticipated litigation is delayed.

sections.title: Power to make up deficiency of court-fees
sections.raw_text: Where the whole or any part of any fee prescribed for any document by the law for the time being in force relating to court-fees has not been paid, the Court may, in its discretion, at any stage, allow the person, by whom such fee is payable, to pay the whole or part, as the case may be, of such court-fee; and upon such payment the document, in respect of which such fee is payable, shall have the same force and effect as if such fee had been paid in the first instance.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 149 gives the Court discretion to allow a litigant to make good any shortfall in the court-fee payable on a document (most commonly the plaint) at any stage of the proceedings, rather than treating an initial underpayment as fatal. If the Court permits this and the deficient fee is duly paid, the document is treated as if the correct fee had been paid right from the very beginning — curing the defect retrospectively, so the suit or proceeding is not lost on a purely technical, curable shortfall in court-fee.
essential_elements: A prescribed court-fee on a document has not been paid, in whole or in part
The Court, in its discretion, allows the person liable to pay the deficient fee to do so at any stage of the proceeding
On such payment, the document is treated as if the correct fee had been paid from the outset
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power is discretionary — the Court is not bound to allow the deficiency to be made up, though it very often does so given the curable, technical nature of the defect
Does not excuse deliberate or persistently contumacious under-valuation aimed at evading court-fees, which Courts may treat differently
breakdown.how_to_read: A vital shield-side and practical drafting-pitfall provision: a suit should never be dismissed outright for court-fee deficiency without the plaintiff first being given an opportunity under Section 149 to make up the shortfall — cite this section promptly if an objection to court-fee sufficiency is raised, whether by the defendant or by the Court's own registry scrutiny.

sections.title: Transfer of business
sections.raw_text: Save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the Court to which the business is so transferred shall have the same powers and shall perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by this Code upon the Court from which the business was so transferred.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 150 ensures administrative continuity when the business (pending cases, jurisdiction, or functions) of one Court is transferred to another Court — for example, due to reorganization of court establishments, redistricting, or abolition/creation of court posts. The Court to which such business is transferred automatically steps into the same powers and duties under the Code that the original Court had, so pending matters and procedural authority continue seamlessly without needing fresh conferral of jurisdiction or powers on the successor Court.
essential_elements: The business of one Court is transferred to another Court (otherwise than as specifically provided elsewhere)
The transferee Court thereupon has the same powers, and must perform the same duties, under the Code as the transferor Court had
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies 'save as otherwise provided' — any specific statutory provision governing a particular transfer scenario differently would override this general default rule
breakdown.how_to_read: A background administrative-continuity provision rarely litigated directly, but useful to cite when questioning whether a newly constituted or redesignated Court has authority over matters pending before its predecessor.

sections.title: Saving of inherent powers of Court
sections.raw_text: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court.
key_terms: abuse of process of the Court

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 151 is one of the most powerful and frequently invoked provisions of the Code, though deceptively short. It does not itself confer any new power on Courts; rather, it 'saves' — preserves and confirms — the inherent powers that civil Courts already possess by virtue of being Courts of justice, powers that exist independently of any express provision in the Code. These inherent powers may be exercised for two overlapping purposes: to secure the ends of justice (i.e., to do complete justice between the parties where the Code's express machinery is silent or inadequate), and to prevent abuse of the Court's own process (i.e., to stop litigants from misusing procedure to achieve an unjust or oppressive result, such as vexatious relitigation, fraud on the Court, or circumventing an express procedural bar). Because inherent powers are residual and extraordinary, courts consistently hold they cannot be used to override an express provision of the Code, to do something the Code specifically prohibits, or as a substitute for an available specific remedy that a party simply failed to invoke in time.
essential_elements: The Code contains no express provision covering the situation, or does not otherwise limit the Court's action in that regard
The order sought is necessary either for the ends of justice, or to prevent abuse of the Court's own process
The power is exercised by the Court itself, in its own discretion, not as an entitlement a party can demand as of right
exceptions_and_qualifications: Inherent power cannot be invoked to do something an express provision of the Code specifically prohibits or regulates differently — it is a gap-filler, not an override
It cannot be used as a backdoor route to circumvent a specific procedural bar or limitation that Parliament has deliberately imposed
It is exercised sparingly and cautiously, reserved for genuinely exceptional situations, not as a routine alternative to the Code's specific remedies
breakdown.how_to_read: Among the most heavily litigated and practically indispensable sections of the Code — always plead Section 151 as a fallback ground where the precise relief sought (e.g., recalling an order obtained by fraud, correcting a genuine but non-'clerical' error, or restraining clear abuse of process) doesn't neatly fit any specific Order/Rule, but never lead with it where a specific provision squarely covers the situation, since courts routinely reject Section 151 applications that are really an attempt to bypass an applicable specific remedy or a missed limitation period.

sections.title: Amendment of judgments, decrees or orders
sections.raw_text: Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in judgments, decrees or orders, or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission, may at any time be corrected by the Court either of its own motion or on the application of any of the parties.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 152 allows a Court to correct purely clerical or arithmetical mistakes, or errors arising from an accidental slip or omission, in a judgment, decree, or order — at any time, either on its own initiative or on a party's application. This is a narrow 'housekeeping' power: it lets the Court fix the record so that it accurately reflects what the Court actually decided, correcting typographical errors, miscalculations, or accidental omissions (such as leaving out a party's name that should clearly have been included based on the judgment's own reasoning). It does not permit the Court to reconsider or alter the substance of what it actually decided — that would require review (Section 114), appeal, or revision, not a Section 152 correction.
essential_elements: The mistake is clerical (e.g., a typographical or copying error) or arithmetical (a calculation error), or the error arises from an accidental slip or omission
The mistake appears in a judgment, decree, or order
Correction may be made at any time — no limitation period applies to this narrow corrective power
The Court may act either suo motu (of its own motion) or on a party's application
exceptions_and_qualifications: Strictly confined to clerical, arithmetical, or accidental-slip errors — it cannot be used to change the Court's actual decision, reasoning, or substantive findings
Not a substitute for review, appeal, or revision where a party disagrees with the merits of the decision itself
breakdown.how_to_read: A frequent, low-friction drafting tool: where a decree contains a plain typo, wrong calculation, or an omission that flows self-evidently from the judgment's reasoning (e.g., the judgment awards interest but the decree's operative part forgets to state the rate), move under Section 152 rather than filing an appeal or review — but be alert that courts will refuse to use Section 152 as a disguised route to reargue or modify the actual decision on the merits.

sections.title: General power to amend
sections.raw_text: The Court may at any time, and on such terms as to costs or otherwise as it may think fit, amend any defect or error in any proceeding in a suit; and all necessary amendments shall be made for the purpose of determining the real question or issue raised by or depending on such proceeding.
key_terms: amendment on terms as to costs

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 153 confers a broad, general power on the Court to amend any defect or error occurring anywhere in a suit's proceedings — not limited to judgments/decrees/orders (which is Section 152's narrower domain) but extending to pleadings, process, and other procedural steps generally. The overriding purpose stated in the section itself is that amendments should be made whenever necessary to determine the real question or issue actually in controversy between the parties — reflecting the broader philosophy that procedure is meant to serve substantive justice, not defeat it on technical defects. The Court can impose terms, typically as to costs, as a condition of allowing such an amendment, to compensate the other side for any prejudice caused by the defect or its correction.
essential_elements: A defect or error exists in any proceeding in a suit
The Court may amend it at any time
The Court may impose terms as to costs or otherwise as a condition of the amendment
The touchstone is whether the amendment is necessary to determine the real question or issue raised by or depending on the proceeding
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power, though general, is still guided by the 'real question or issue' standard — it is not a licence for unlimited procedural rewriting untethered to genuinely resolving the actual controversy
Courts typically also weigh prejudice to the opposite party and delay, awarding costs to offset any disadvantage caused by late correction
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 153 works alongside the more specific Order VI Rule 17 (amendment of pleadings) as a general reservoir of amending power for procedural defects not squarely covered by a specific Order/Rule — cite it when a purely technical or formal defect (short of a defective pleading needing Rule 17) threatens to derail the real merits of the case.

sections.title: Power to amend decree or order where appeal is summarily dismissed
sections.raw_text: (1) Where an appeal is summarily dismissed under rule 11 of Order XLI, the Court which passed the decree or order appealed from shall have power to amend, in accordance with the provisions of section 152, such decree or order notwithstanding the fact that the appeal from such decree or order has been dismissed. (2) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall affect any right which the appellant may have to institute a suit for the purpose of correcting a decree or order on the ground of any error or omission of the nature referred to in section 152, but no such suit shall be instituted in any Court in which an appeal against the decree or order might have been brought under any law.
key_terms: trial court's power despite dismissed appeal

breakdown.plain_summary: Normally, once an appellate court has dismissed an appeal (even summarily, without formally admitting it or issuing notice to the other side, under Order XLI Rule 11), a question can arise whether the trial Court still retains jurisdiction to correct clerical/arithmetical errors under Section 152 in the decree that was the subject of that (now-dismissed) appeal — since the decree's finality might seem tied up with the appellate court's dismissal order. Section 153A resolves this doubt directly: the trial Court that passed the original decree or order keeps its Section 152 correcting power intact, notwithstanding that an appeal against that decree/order was summarily dismissed. Sub-section (2) separately preserves an appellant's right to institute a fresh suit to correct such an error, but only in a Court where an appeal against the decree/order could not have been brought — i.e., it prevents using a fresh suit as a backdoor route in a Court where an appeal was in fact available and already pursued (and summarily dismissed).
essential_elements: An appeal against a decree or order was summarily dismissed under Order XLI Rule 11
The trial Court that passed the decree/order retains its Section 152 power to correct clerical/arithmetical mistakes or accidental slips/omissions in it
An appellant's separate right to sue for such correction survives, but only in a Court where an appeal against the decree/order could not have been brought
exceptions_and_qualifications: Confined specifically to the situation of a summarily dismissed appeal under Order XLI Rule 11 — not appeals dismissed after full hearing on the merits
Sub-section (2)'s preserved suit-right is itself qualified — it cannot be exercised in a Court where an appeal was actually available (to prevent forum-shopping around the dismissed appeal)
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow but useful clarification for practitioners: don't assume a summarily dismissed appeal strips the trial Court of its ordinary Section 152 correcting power over its own decree — that power survives intact, and a fresh Section 152 application to the trial Court remains the right route rather than a new suit.

sections.title: Place of trial to be deemed to be open Court
sections.raw_text: The place in which any Civil Court is held for the purpose of trying any suit shall be deemed to be an open Court, to which the public generally may have access so far as the same can conveniently contain them: Provided that the presiding Judge may, if he thinks fit, order at any stage of any inquiry into or trial of any particular case, that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access to, or be or remain in, the room or building used by the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 153B codifies the fundamental principle of open justice for civil trials — the place where a Civil Court sits to try a suit is deemed an 'open Court', meaning members of the public generally have a right of access to observe proceedings, subject only to practical space constraints. This transparency principle promotes public confidence in the fairness of judicial proceedings. The proviso gives the presiding Judge a discretionary power to depart from this default at any stage of an inquiry or trial in a particular case, by ordering that the public generally, or a specific person, be excluded from the courtroom — used, for example, in sensitive matrimonial or matters involving minors, trade secrets, or other circumstances where open-court proceedings could cause disproportionate harm.
essential_elements: The place where a Civil Court sits to try a suit is deemed an open Court
The public generally has a right of access, subject to the physical capacity of the room/building
The presiding Judge may, in a particular case and at any stage, order exclusion of the public generally or a specific person from the courtroom
exceptions_and_qualifications: The open-court default can be displaced entirely at the Judge's discretion via the proviso — it is not an absolute, unqualified right of public access
Access is inherently limited by physical capacity ('so far as the same can conveniently contain them')
breakdown.how_to_read: Relevant when seeking, or resisting, an in-camera (closed-court) hearing — for example, in cases involving sensitive personal, matrimonial, or commercially confidential material — cite Section 153B's proviso as the statutory basis for requesting exclusion of the public, supported by specific facts showing why open proceedings would cause disproportionate prejudice.

sections.title: [Saving of present right of appeal.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Section 154, which originally dealt with the saving of an existing right of appeal on the Code's commencement, has been repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938), its transitional purpose having been spent long ago.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 154 was a transitional saving clause protecting rights of appeal that already existed when the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 first came into force, ensuring the new Code didn't retroactively strip away appeal rights litigants already had under the prior law. Having served its one-time transitional purpose at the Code's commencement over a century ago, it was formally repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938, and now survives only as a numbering placeholder.
essential_elements: Repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938)
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a numbering-only placeholder in the Code's section sequence
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a numbering-only placeholder with no continuing legal effect; its transitional function was exhausted decades ago.

sections.title: [Amendment of certain Acts.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Section 155, which originally made consequential amendments to certain other Acts upon the Code's commencement, has been repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938), its amending purpose having been fully spent.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 155 originally amended various other statutes to align them with the newly enacted Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Once those consequential amendments took effect at the Code's commencement, the section had no further work to do, and it was accordingly repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938. It now survives only as a placeholder in the Code's numbering.
essential_elements: Repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938)
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a numbering-only placeholder in the Code's section sequence
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a numbering-only placeholder with no continuing legal effect; the consequential amendments it once made are now embedded in the amended statutes themselves.

sections.title: [Repeals.] Repealed.
sections.raw_text: Section 156, which originally listed the earlier enactments repealed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 upon its commencement, has itself been repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938), its repealing purpose having been fully spent.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 156 was the Code's own repealing schedule, listing the pre-1908 enactments that the new Code superseded when it came into force. Having accomplished that one-time repealing function long ago, the section itself was subsequently repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938, and now survives only as a numbering placeholder.
essential_elements: Repealed by the Repealing Act, 1938 (1 of 1938)
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a numbering-only placeholder in the Code's section sequence
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a numbering-only placeholder with no continuing legal effect; see Section 158 for the Code's ongoing rule for construing references to enactments this section once repealed.

sections.title: Continuance of orders under repealed enactments
sections.raw_text: All orders made, and rules framed, under any enactment hereby repealed and in force at the commencement of this Code shall, so far as they are not inconsistent with this Code, be deemed, respectively, to have been made and framed under this Code, and to be continued accordingly.
key_terms: continuance of prior orders and rules

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 157 is a transitional continuity provision ensuring that orders made, and rules framed, under the pre-1908 enactments that the Code repealed did not simply vanish or need to be remade from scratch the moment the new Code came into force. Instead, so long as those old orders and rules are not inconsistent with the new Code, they are deemed to have been made or framed under the Code itself and continue in force accordingly — providing a seamless transition from the old procedural regime to the new one, without any interruption or need to reissue every existing order and rule.
essential_elements: An order was made, or rules were framed, under a pre-1908 enactment that the Code repealed
That order or rule was in force at the commencement of the Code
It is not inconsistent with the Code
It is then deemed to have been made/framed under the Code itself, and continues accordingly
exceptions_and_qualifications: The continuity is conditional — only orders/rules not inconsistent with the new Code survive this deeming provision; anything genuinely inconsistent falls away
breakdown.how_to_read: Now of essentially historical interest only, given the Code has been in continuous force for over a century, but it establishes the interpretive template for how the Code handles transitions from repealed regimes — useful analogically when arguing continuity of subordinate rules/orders across any later legislative repeal-and-replace scenario.

sections.title: Reference to Code of Civil Procedure and other repealed enactments
sections.raw_text: In all enactments passed before the commencement of this Code in which reference is made to any section or provision of the Code of Civil Procedure, or in which reference is made to the number of any section of the Code of Civil Procedure which section has, with or without amendment, been re-enacted by this Code, such reference shall, unless a different intention appears, be construed as a reference made to the section or provision so re-enacted.

breakdown.plain_summary: The final numbered section of the Code addresses how older statutes — enacted before this Code came into force — that refer to sections or provisions of the earlier Code of Civil Procedure should be read now that this 1908 Code has re-enacted (with or without amendments) those same provisions under possibly different numbering. Section 158 lays down a sensible default interpretive rule: unless a contrary intention appears, such a cross-reference in the older enactment is to be read as pointing to the corresponding re-enacted section or provision of this Code — so that references in old legislation continue to make sense and correctly track the current, applicable provision rather than becoming orphaned pointers to a repealed and now-defunct earlier Code.
essential_elements: An enactment passed before the commencement of this Code refers to a section or provision of the earlier Code of Civil Procedure
That earlier section has been re-enacted (with or without amendment) by this Code
Unless a different intention appears in that older enactment, the reference is construed as pointing to the corresponding re-enacted provision of this Code
exceptions_and_qualifications: The default construction yields wherever the older enactment itself shows a different intention
Applies specifically to references to the Code of Civil Procedure's own provisions, not references to other unrelated repealed statutes
breakdown.how_to_read: A pure statutory-interpretation aid, useful chiefly when construing older legislation (pre-1908) that cross-refers to Code of Civil Procedure sections by number — confirms the reference should be read as pointing to this Code's corresponding current provision, completing the Code's numbered Sections 1 through 158; the First Schedule's Orders and Rules (Order I onward) follow immediately after and fall outside this numbered-Sections series.
